items.meaning: A common, informal way to ask someone how they are doing or how their life is going.
items.example: Hi Mark, long time no see! How are things with you these days?
items.plain: Hi Mark, long time no see! How are you doing these days?
items.note: Very common, informal greeting. Good for starting a casual conversation with someone you know.

items.text: What have you been up to
items.form: What have you been up to
items.meaning: An informal question asking what someone has been doing recently.
items.example: It's been a while, Sarah. What have you been up to since we last met?
items.plain: It's been a while, Sarah. What have you been doing since we last met?
items.note: Casual and friendly. Excellent for reconnecting with acquaintances or friends.

items.meaning: To learn about recent events or news from someone you haven't spoken to in a while.
items.example: It was great to catch up on all your news from the trip.
items.plain: It was great to hear all your news from the trip.
items.note: Used when you want to hear what someone has been doing. Often followed by 'news' or 'gossip'.

items.meaning: A friendly greeting expressing pleasure at meeting or seeing someone.
items.example: Oh, hello! It's good to see you again after all this time.
items.plain: Oh, hello! I'm happy to see you again after all this time.
items.note: Standard polite greeting, suitable for both formal and informal situations.

items.meaning: A casual question to ask someone about their current day.
items.example: Morning, Tom. How's your day going so far?
items.plain: Morning, Tom. How is your day so far?
items.note: Common small talk opener, especially in the morning or early afternoon.

items.meaning: An informal response meaning things are generally good or satisfactory.
items.example: How are you doing? Oh, can't complain, just busy with work.
items.plain: How are you doing? Oh, I'm doing fine, just busy with work.
items.note: A very common, understated positive response. Sounds natural and modest.

items.meaning: A polite way to introduce a question or a tentative suggestion.
items.example: I was just wondering if you'd heard anything about the new project.
items.plain: I wanted to ask if you'd heard anything about the new project.
items.note: Softens a question, making it less direct. Useful for gentle inquiries.

items.meaning: A common way to ask for someone's opinion on a topic.
items.example: So, what do you think of the new office layout?
items.plain: So, what's your opinion on the new office layout?
items.note: Direct but polite way to invite someone to share their views.

items.meaning: An expression of agreement, acknowledging the validity of someone's idea.
items.example: You're right, that's a good point about the timing of the meeting.
items.plain: You're right, that's a valid idea about the timing of the meeting.
items.note: Shows you're listening and value their input. Encourages further conversation.

items.meaning: An expression indicating understanding of someone's perspective or argument.
items.example: Ah, I see what you mean now; the earlier deadline makes more sense.
items.plain: Ah, I understand your point now; the earlier deadline makes more sense.
items.note: Commonly used to show comprehension, even if you don't fully agree.

items.meaning: An informal way to introduce your personal opinion or suggestion.
items.example: If you ask me, they should have started this project sooner.
items.plain: In my opinion, they should have started this project sooner.
items.note: Adds a personal touch to an opinion. Can sound a little strong if overused.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a frank or sincere statement, sometimes a mild criticism.
items.example: To be honest, I'm not entirely happy with the new policy.
items.plain: Frankly, I'm not entirely happy with the new policy.
items.note: Signals sincerity. Can soften a negative comment or introduce a personal feeling.

items.meaning: A polite way to express disagreement or uncertainty without being confrontational.
items.example: I'm not sure about that; I thought the report said something different.
items.plain: I don't agree with that; I thought the report said something different.
items.note: A gentle way to express doubt or a differing opinion. Very useful in polite conversation.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a related thought or anecdote triggered by the current conversation.
items.example: Oh, that reminds me of a similar situation I had last year.
items.plain: Oh, that makes me think of a similar situation I had last year.
items.note: Excellent for keeping a conversation flowing by linking topics.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a new topic that is related to what was just said.
items.example: We were talking about holidays. Speaking of which, have you booked your trip yet?
items.plain: We were talking about holidays. By the way, have you booked your trip yet?
items.note: Smoothly transitions to a related subject. Very common in natural speech.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a new, often unrelated, piece of information or question.
items.example: I'm heading to the shop. By the way, do you need anything?
items.plain: I'm heading to the shop. Also, do you need anything?
items.note: A very common way to change the subject or add an afterthought.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a contrasting point or an alternative perspective.
items.example: It's a long commute, but on the other hand, the job is very rewarding.
items.plain: It's a long commute, but alternatively, the job is very rewarding.
items.note: Helps present a balanced view. Useful for discussing pros and cons.

items.meaning: An emphatic expression of complete agreement with someone's statement.
items.example: That's exactly how I feel. I couldn't agree more with your assessment.
items.plain: That's exactly how I feel. I completely agree with your assessment.
items.note: Strong agreement. Use when you genuinely feel the same way.

items.meaning: An expression of mild disappointment or sympathy for an unfortunate situation.
items.example: Oh, you missed the concert? That's a shame, it was fantastic.
items.plain: Oh, you missed the concert? That's too bad, it was fantastic.
items.note: Commonly used to express regret or sympathy for minor negative events.

items.meaning: An informal way of saying 'no problem' or 'it's alright'.
items.example: Thanks for helping out. No worries at all, happy to do it.
items.plain: Thanks for helping out. No problem at all, happy to do it.
items.note: Very common in Australian English, now widely used in British and American English.

items.meaning: A polite way to say goodbye, indicating you enjoyed the interaction.
items.example: Well, I must be going. It's been a pleasure chatting with you.
items.plain: Well, I must be going. I enjoyed chatting with you.
items.note: A polite and slightly formal way to end a conversation, especially with new acquaintances.

items.meaning: A common, polite way to signal that you need to leave.
items.example: It's getting late, so I should get going now.
items.plain: It's getting late, so I need to leave now.
items.note: A gentle way to exit a conversation without being abrupt.

items.text: It was nice talking to you
items.form: It was nice talking to you
items.meaning: A polite closing remark when ending a conversation.
items.example: Right, I'll catch you later. It was nice talking to you.
items.plain: Right, I'll catch you later. I enjoyed our conversation.
items.note: Standard polite farewell, suitable for most casual and semi-formal interactions.

items.meaning: An informal, general farewell wishing someone a good day, evening, etc.
items.example: See you tomorrow! Have a good one!
items.plain: See you tomorrow! Have a good day!
items.note: Very common and friendly. Can refer to a day, evening, weekend, or general time.

items.meaning: A common, friendly farewell, wishing someone well.
items.example: I'm off now. Take care, and see you next week!
items.plain: I'm off now. Be well, and see you next week!
items.note: A warm and personal way to say goodbye, suitable for friends and colleagues.

items.meaning: A polite way to express regret when stating something you must do, often leave.
items.example: I'm afraid I have to run, I have another meeting starting soon.
items.plain: Unfortunately, I must leave, I have another meeting starting soon.
items.note: Softens the message, making it sound more apologetic or regretful.

items.meaning: Used to express strong anticipation or excitement about a future event.
items.example: I'm really looking forward to the team dinner next month.
items.plain: I'm very excited about the team dinner next month.
items.note: A common and enthusiastic way to talk about future plans.

items.meaning: Used to express an inference or impression based on what someone has said.
items.example: It sounds like you had a fantastic holiday in Italy.
items.plain: It seems you had a fantastic holiday in Italy.
items.note: Shows you're listening and processing information. Good for empathetic responses.

items.meaning: Used to check if the listener understands or agrees with your point.
items.example: It's just a bit overwhelming sometimes, you know what I mean?
items.plain: It's just a bit overwhelming sometimes, do you understand?
items.note: Very common in informal speech. Can be a filler or a genuine check for understanding.

items.meaning: An informal way to say you are leaving briefly, usually for a short errand.
items.example: I'm just popping out to grab a coffee, back in five.
items.plain: I'm just going out briefly to grab a coffee, back in five.
items.note: Casual and friendly. Implies a quick return. Common in office settings.

items.meaning: A common question to start a conversation on Monday morning.
items.example: Good morning! How was your weekend, did you do anything fun?
items.plain: Good morning! What did you do this weekend, did you do anything fun?
items.note: Standard small talk for the start of the week. Expect a brief, light answer.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a piece of news or gossip and ask if the listener knows.
items.example: Did you hear about the new cafe opening down the street?
items.plain: Are you aware of the new cafe opening down the street?
items.note: Good for sharing news or starting a discussion on a current event.

items.meaning: A polite and indirect way to ask a question or make a request.
items.example: I was wondering if you'd be free for a quick chat later.
items.plain: Would you be free for a quick chat later?
items.note: Very polite and less demanding than a direct question. Useful for requests.

items.meaning: An expression used when you discover an unexpected connection with someone.
items.example: You know my cousin? Wow, it's a small world!
items.plain: You know my cousin? Wow, what an unexpected connection!
items.note: Common and friendly. Expresses surprise at coincidences.

items.meaning: An expression of surprise at an unexpected occurrence or connection.
items.example: We both went to the same university? What a coincidence!
items.plain: We both went to the same university? How unexpected!
items.note: Similar to 'It's a small world', but can be used for any surprising event.

items.meaning: Used to indicate that you are going to do something very soon.
items.example: I'm just about to head out for lunch, want to join?
items.plain: I'm going to head out for lunch very soon, want to join?
items.note: Common for describing immediate future actions. Can be an invitation.

items.meaning: A polite way to ask someone for their opinion or experience of something.
items.example: How do you find working from home these days?
items.plain: What's your experience of working from home these days?
items.note: Asks for a general impression or evaluation. More nuanced than 'What do you think?'

items.meaning: An expression of pleasure or relief upon hearing good news.
items.example: You got the promotion? I'm glad to hear that, congratulations!
items.plain: You got the promotion? I'm happy to hear that, congratulations!
items.note: A warm and supportive response to positive news. Very common.

items.meaning: An expression of sympathy or regret upon hearing bad news.
items.example: Your flight was cancelled? I'm sorry to hear that, what a hassle.
items.plain: Your flight was cancelled? I regret to hear that, what a hassle.
items.note: A standard empathetic response to negative news. Polite and caring.

items.meaning: A common expression to indicate tiredness or that the day has been challenging.
items.example: Phew, it's been a long day, I'm ready to go home.
items.plain: Phew, this day has been tiring, I'm ready to go home.
items.note: Relatable and often used to signal the end of a work day or a desire to rest.

items.meaning: Used to indicate that you are very close to finishing a task.
items.example: I'm just about done with this report, then I can join you.
items.plain: I'm almost finished with this report, then I can join you.
items.note: Useful for coordinating activities or managing expectations about your availability.

items.meaning: A common question to ask about someone's upcoming activities or intentions.
items.example: What are your plans for the long weekend?
items.plain: What will you do during the long weekend?
items.note: Good for light conversation about future leisure time. Avoid overly personal questions.

items.text: I was just thinking about you
items.form: I was just thinking about you
items.meaning: A friendly expression used when you encounter someone you were recently considering.
items.example: Oh, hi! I was just thinking about you and that project.
items.plain: Oh, hi! I was recently considering you and that project.
items.note: Creates an immediate connection and makes the other person feel acknowledged.

items.meaning: A general question to ask about the status of a specific project or situation.
items.example: How's everything going with the new software implementation?
items.plain: What's the status of the new software implementation?
items.note: Good for following up on a topic previously discussed. Shows interest.

items.meaning: A common way to express uncertainty or lack of knowledge about something.
items.example: I'm not really sure what time the event starts, I'll check.
items.plain: I don't know what time the event starts, I'll check.
items.note: Polite and honest. Avoids making up information.

items.meaning: A promise to provide updates as new information becomes available.
items.example: I'll let you know about the meeting time. I'll keep you posted.
items.plain: I'll let you know about the meeting time. I'll give you updates.
items.note: Common and professional. Assures the other person they won't be left out of the loop.

items.meaning: Used to offer help or invite someone to inform you about something.
items.example: Let me know if you need any help with the presentation.
items.plain: Tell me if you need any help with the presentation.
items.note: A polite and helpful offer. Encourages communication.

items.meaning: An informal way to announce that you are leaving a place.
items.example: Right, I'm just heading off now, see you tomorrow.
items.plain: Right, I'm leaving now, see you tomorrow.
items.note: Casual and common. Good for signaling departure from work or a social gathering.

items.meaning: Used to acknowledge that a significant amount of time has passed since last meeting.
items.example: Wow, it's been a while since we last saw each other!
items.plain: Wow, a long time has passed since we last saw each other!
items.note: A friendly way to start a conversation with someone you haven't seen in ages.

items.meaning: An informal and friendly way to ask someone how they are doing generally.
items.example: Hey, long time no talk! How's life treating you these days?
items.plain: Hey, long time no talk! How are you doing these days?
items.note: More personal than 'How are things?'. Good for closer acquaintances.

items.meaning: Used to explain your current goal or intention, often with a hint of effort.
items.example: I'm just trying to finish this report before the deadline.
items.plain: My goal is to finish this report before the deadline.
items.note: Explains your current focus. Can be used to politely decline an interruption.

items.meaning: A polite way to say you don't enjoy or have an interest in something.
items.example: Thanks for the invite, but I'm not really into hiking.
items.plain: Thanks for the invite, but I don't really enjoy hiking.
items.note: A gentle way to decline an offer or express disinterest without being rude.

items.meaning: A neutral response indicating you've heard something new or thought-provoking.
items.example: Oh, you're moving to Canada? That's interesting!
items.plain: Oh, you're moving to Canada? That's new information!
items.note: Can be genuine or a polite filler. Use with appropriate tone to avoid sounding sarcastic.

items.meaning: Used to indicate that you are on the verge of departing.
items.example: I'm just about to leave for my appointment, so I can't chat long.
items.plain: I'm going to leave very soon for my appointment, so I can't chat long.
items.note: A clear signal that you need to end the conversation soon.

items.meaning: A friendly expression used when you've had a chance to talk and share news.
items.example: Well, it's good to catch up, let's do it again soon.
items.plain: Well, it's good to talk and share news, let's do it again soon.
items.note: Common closing remark after a conversation with someone you haven't seen in a while.

items.meaning: A very polite and tentative way to ask a question or make a suggestion.
items.example: I'm just wondering if you'd considered a different approach.
items.plain: I wanted to ask if you'd considered a different approach.
items.note: Softer than 'I was wondering if'. Good for sensitive topics or suggestions.

items.meaning: An informal question asking for recent updates or news in someone's life.
items.example: Hey, long time no see! What's new with you?
items.plain: Hey, long time no see! What has happened recently in your life?
items.note: Casual and friendly. Good for starting a conversation with an acquaintance.

items.meaning: Used to explain your current effort or goal, often related to understanding or achieving something.
items.example: I'm just trying to get my head around this new software.
items.plain: I'm trying to understand this new software.
items.note: Explains a current struggle or learning process. Can invite empathy or advice.

items.meaning: A polite way to say you don't understand what someone is explaining.
items.example: Could you explain that again? I'm not sure I follow.
items.plain: Could you explain that again? I don't understand.
items.note: More polite than 'I don't understand'. Good for asking for clarification.

items.meaning: Used to indicate that you are almost prepared for something.
items.example: Give me five minutes, I'm just about ready to go.
items.plain: Give me five minutes, I'm almost prepared to go.
items.note: Common for coordinating departures or starting activities.

items.meaning: An informal way to say you are making a brief, quick visit.
items.example: Hi, I'm just popping in to say hello before my next meeting.
items.plain: Hi, I'm visiting briefly to say hello before my next meeting.
items.note: Casual and friendly. Implies a short stay. Common in office or neighborly contexts.

items.meaning: Used to briefly contact someone to see how they are or how things are going.
items.example: Hi, I'm just checking in to see if you received my email.
items.plain: Hi, I'm contacting you briefly to see if you received my email.
items.note: Common in professional and personal contexts for a quick follow-up.

items.text: It's been a pleasure meeting you
items.form: It's been a pleasure meeting you
items.meaning: A polite closing remark when ending a conversation with someone you met for the first time.
items.example: Well, I must go. It's been a pleasure meeting you, Sarah.
items.plain: Well, I must go. I enjoyed meeting you, Sarah.
items.note: Standard polite farewell for new acquaintances. Slightly more formal than 'talking to you'.

items.text: I'm just trying to figure out
items.form: I'm just trying to figure out
items.meaning: Used to explain that you are currently attempting to understand or solve something.
items.example: I'm just trying to figure out how to use this new coffee machine.
items.plain: I'm trying to understand how to use this new coffee machine.
items.note: Common for explaining a current mental task or problem-solving effort.

items.meaning: An informal question asking what someone is currently doing or planning.
items.example: Hey, what are you up to this evening?
items.plain: Hey, what are you doing this evening?
items.note: Very casual and friendly. Can be used to initiate plans or just chat.

items.meaning: Used to indicate that you are on the verge of beginning an activity.
items.example: I'm just about to start my presentation, wish me luck!
items.plain: I'm going to start my presentation very soon, wish me luck!
items.note: Common for signaling the imminent beginning of a task or event.

items.text: It's a bit of a long story
items.form: It's a bit of a long story
items.meaning: Used to indicate that an explanation is complicated or lengthy, often to avoid giving details.
items.example: Why did I change jobs? Oh, it's a bit of a long story.
items.plain: Why did I change jobs? Oh, the explanation is complicated.
items.note: Polite way to deflect a question without being rude, implying you don't have time or desire to explain.

items.meaning: Used to indicate that you have only recently begun an activity.
items.example: I'm just getting started on this project, so I don't have much to report.
items.plain: I've only recently begun this project, so I don't have much to report.
items.note: Common for setting expectations about progress or availability.

items.text: I'm just trying to make sure
items.form: I'm just trying to make sure
items.meaning: Used to explain your current effort to confirm or verify something.
items.example: I'm just trying to make sure all the details are correct.
items.plain: I'm trying to confirm all the details are correct.
items.note: Explains a careful or diligent approach to a task.

items.meaning: Used to indicate that you are very close to completing a specific task.
items.example: I'm just about done with this email, then I'm free.
items.plain: I'm almost finished with this email, then I'm free.
items.note: Specific version of 'I'm just about done'. Useful for managing expectations.

items.meaning: A common phrase to explain why you might be tired or haven't done much else.
items.example: I haven't had time for hobbies, it's been a busy week at work.
items.plain: I haven't had time for hobbies, my work week was very active.
items.note: Relatable and often used as a mild excuse or explanation for lack of free time.

items.text: I'm just trying to catch up
items.form: I'm just trying to catch up
items.meaning: Used to explain that you are working to get up to date after a period of absence or backlog.
items.example: Sorry I'm slow, I'm just trying to catch up on emails after my holiday.
items.plain: Sorry I'm slow, I'm trying to get up to date on emails after my holiday.
items.note: Common in professional settings. Explains a current focus on clearing a backlog.

items.text: I'm just about to head out
items.form: I'm just about to head out
items.meaning: Used to indicate that you are on the verge of leaving a place.
items.example: I'm just about to head out for the day, see you tomorrow.
items.plain: I'm going to leave for the day very soon, see you tomorrow.
items.note: A clear signal that you are departing. Similar to 'I'm just heading off'.

items.text: I'm just trying to get organised
items.form: I'm just trying to get organised
items.meaning: Used to explain that you are currently making an effort to arrange or plan things.
items.example: I'm just trying to get organised for the big presentation next week.
items.plain: I'm trying to arrange everything for the big presentation next week.
items.note: Explains a current focus on preparation and planning.

items.text: It's been a pleasure working with you
items.form: It's been a pleasure working with you
items.meaning: A polite closing remark, especially when a project or collaboration ends.
items.example: As this project wraps up, it's been a pleasure working with you all.
items.plain: As this project wraps up, I enjoyed working with you all.
items.note: Professional and polite. Good for ending a work-related interaction.

items.text: I'm just trying to get a handle on
items.form: I'm just trying to get a handle on
items.meaning: Used to explain that you are currently attempting to understand or manage a situation.
items.example: I'm just trying to get a handle on all these new responsibilities.
items.plain: I'm trying to understand and manage all these new responsibilities.
items.note: Implies a learning curve or a challenge in gaining control.

items.text: I'm just about to call it a day
items.form: I'm just about to call it a day
items.meaning: An informal way to say you are about to stop working for the day.
items.example: I'm just about to call it a day, I'm exhausted.
items.plain: I'm going to stop working for the day very soon, I'm exhausted.
items.note: Very common and casual. Signals the end of the workday.

items.text: I'm just trying to get some work done
items.form: I'm just trying to get some work done
items.meaning: Used to politely indicate that you are busy and need to focus on your tasks.
items.example: Sorry, I can't chat long, I'm just trying to get some work done.
items.plain: Sorry, I can't chat long, I'm busy with my tasks.
items.note: A polite way to end or avoid a conversation when you need to concentrate.

items.meaning: A common phrase to express satisfaction with what you've accomplished.
items.example: I managed to finish three reports, it's been a productive day.
items.plain: I managed to finish three reports, this day was very fruitful.
items.note: Positive and professional. Good for light conversation about work.

items.text: I'm just trying to get my head around
items.form: I'm just trying to get my head around
items.meaning: Used to explain that you are currently attempting to understand a complex idea or situation.
items.example: I'm just trying to get my head around the new tax regulations.
items.plain: I'm trying to understand the new tax regulations.
items.note: Implies a mental effort to grasp something difficult. Very common.

items.text: I'm just about to grab some lunch
items.form: I'm just about to grab some lunch
items.meaning: Used to indicate that you are about to go and eat lunch.
items.example: I'm just about to grab some lunch, want to join me?
items.plain: I'm going to get some lunch very soon, want to join me?
items.note: Common and casual. Can be an invitation or an explanation for leaving.

items.text: I'm just trying to sort out
items.form: I'm just trying to sort out
items.meaning: Used to explain that you are currently attempting to organize or resolve something.
items.example: I'm just trying to sort out my travel arrangements for next month.
items.plain: I'm trying to organize my travel arrangements for next month.
items.note: Common for explaining a current task involving organization or problem-solving.

items.text: It's been a pleasure having you
items.form: It's been a pleasure having you
items.meaning: A polite closing remark from a host to a guest, indicating enjoyment of their visit.
items.example: Thanks for coming, it's been a pleasure having you over.
items.plain: Thanks for coming, I enjoyed your visit.
items.note: Used by a host. Polite and warm. Suitable for social gatherings.

items.text: I'm just trying to finish up
items.form: I'm just trying to finish up
items.meaning: Used to indicate that you are in the final stages of completing a task.
items.example: I'm just trying to finish up this email, then I'm all yours.
items.plain: I'm trying to complete this email, then I'm all yours.
items.note: Common for signaling that you'll be available soon after a task.

items.text: I'm just about to head home
items.form: I'm just about to head home
items.meaning: Used to indicate that you are on the verge of leaving to go home.
items.example: It's late, I'm just about to head home.
items.plain: It's late, I'm going to leave for home very soon.
items.note: A clear signal that you are departing for the day. Very common.

items.text: I'm just trying to get a feel for
items.form: I'm just trying to get a feel for
items.meaning: Used to explain that you are currently attempting to understand the general nature of something.
items.example: I'm just trying to get a feel for the team dynamics.
items.plain: I'm trying to understand the general nature of the team dynamics.
items.note: Implies an exploratory process of understanding a situation or environment.

items.meaning: Used to acknowledge that a long time has passed since a particular event.
items.example: It's been a while since I last visited my hometown.
items.plain: A long time has passed since I last visited my hometown.
items.note: Common for reminiscing or explaining a gap in activity.

items.text: I'm just trying to get organised for
items.form: I'm just trying to get organised for
items.meaning: Used to explain that you are currently preparing or arranging things for a specific event.
items.example: I'm just trying to get organised for the conference next week.
items.plain: I'm trying to prepare everything for the conference next week.
items.note: Specific version of 'I'm just trying to get organised'. Focuses on a future event.

items.text: I'm just about to start on
items.form: I'm just about to start on
items.meaning: Used to indicate that you are on the verge of beginning a specific task or project.
items.example: I'm just about to start on the new marketing campaign.
items.plain: I'm going to begin the new marketing campaign very soon.
items.note: Specific version of 'I'm just about to start'. Focuses on a particular task.

items.text: I'm just trying to get everything ready
items.form: I'm just trying to get everything ready
items.meaning: Used to explain that you are currently making an effort to prepare all necessary items.
items.example: I'm just trying to get everything ready for the client meeting.
items.plain: I'm trying to prepare all necessary items for the client meeting.
items.note: Common for explaining a current focus on comprehensive preparation.

items.text: It's been a pleasure chatting with you
items.form: It's been a pleasure chatting with you
items.meaning: A polite closing remark when ending a casual conversation.
items.example: Well, I should go. It's been a pleasure chatting with you.
items.plain: Well, I should go. I enjoyed our casual conversation.
items.note: Friendly and polite. Suitable for informal interactions with acquaintances.

items.text: I'm just trying to get through
items.form: I'm just trying to get through
items.meaning: Used to explain that you are currently attempting to complete a difficult or lengthy task.
items.example: I'm just trying to get through this pile of paperwork.
items.plain: I'm trying to complete this large amount of paperwork.
items.note: Implies a struggle or a large volume of work that needs to be done.

items.text: I'm just about to wrap up
items.form: I'm just about to wrap up
items.meaning: Used to indicate that you are in the final stages of completing a task or meeting.
items.example: I'm just about to wrap up this call, then I'm free.
items.plain: I'm going to finish this call very soon, then I'm free.
items.note: Common in professional settings for signaling the end of a task or interaction.

items.text: I'm just trying to get a sense of
items.form: I'm just trying to get a sense of
items.meaning: Used to explain that you are currently attempting to understand the general impression or feeling of something.
items.example: I'm just trying to get a sense of the team's mood.
items.plain: I'm trying to understand the general feeling of the team.
items.note: Implies an effort to gauge an atmosphere or overall impression.

items.text: It's been a pleasure working alongside you
items.form: It's been a pleasure working alongside you
items.meaning: A polite closing remark, especially when a collaborative project ends.
items.example: As the project concludes, it's been a pleasure working alongside you.
items.plain: As the project concludes, I enjoyed collaborating with you.
items.note: Professional and polite. Emphasizes collaboration. Slightly more formal.

items.text: I'm just trying to get everything in order
items.form: I'm just trying to get everything in order
items.meaning: Used to explain that you are currently making an effort to organize and arrange things properly.
items.example: I'm just trying to get everything in order before I leave for vacation.
items.plain: I'm trying to organize and arrange everything properly before I leave for vacation.
items.note: Common for explaining a current focus on thorough organization.

items.text: I'm just about to head out the door
items.form: I'm just about to head out the door
items.meaning: Used to indicate that you are literally on the verge of leaving a place.
items.example: I'm just about to head out the door, so I'll call you later.
items.plain: I'm going to leave right now, so I'll call you later.
items.note: Very clear signal of imminent departure. Often used to cut a conversation short.

items.text: I'm just about to call it a night
items.form: I'm just about to call it a night
items.meaning: An informal way to say you are about to stop an activity or go to bed for the evening.
items.example: It's getting late, I'm just about to call it a night.
items.plain: It's getting late, I'm going to stop my activities for the evening.
items.note: Very common and casual. Signals the end of the evening's activities.

items.text: I'm just trying to get my bearings
items.form: I'm just trying to get my bearings
items.meaning: Used to explain that you are currently attempting to understand your position or situation.
items.example: I'm new to the city, so I'm just trying to get my bearings.
items.plain: I'm new to the city, so I'm trying to understand my position and surroundings.
items.note: Implies a process of orientation, either literally or figuratively in a new situation.

items.text: I'm just about to get started on
items.form: I'm just about to get started on
items.meaning: Used to indicate that you are on the verge of beginning a specific task or project.
items.example: I'm just about to get started on the quarterly report.
items.plain: I'm going to begin the quarterly report very soon.
items.note: Emphasizes the initiation of a particular task. Very common.
